deep.reconstruction:
Context: E260 models pipe friction as proportional to the local pressure, in the manner of Coulomb solid friction. The pressure p is measured as a water-height. Over a length ds of a cylindrical tube of cross-section ff, the friction force is ∝ α·p·f·ds, since the perimeter is ∝ f. Dividing by the mass per unit length, ∝ ff, gives the steady-flow pressure law dp/ds = cos φ − (α/f) p, where φ is the angle of the tube with the vertical. Integrating over a tube of length a gives p_end = p_start·e^{−αa/f} + (f/α)(1 − e^{−αa/f}) cos φ. For α → 0 this reduces to hydrostatics, p_end = p_start + a cos φ.

On the previous pages Euler treated a two-tube system. Here (§34) he generalises to a canal made of several cylindrical tubes, each inclined arbitrarily:
- Tube AF: length a, cross-section ff, angle ε with the vertical.
- Tube BC: length b, cross-section gg, angle ζ.
- Tube CD: length c, cross-section hh, angle η.
- Tube DE: length d, cross-section ii, angle θ.
- Orifice EE: area kk (earlier called hh).

§35 introduces the following quantities.
- v is the velocity-height of the jet at the orifice. By continuity, the velocity-height in a section of area ff is k^4 v/f^4.
- The pressures (as heights) at the section entrances are l, P, Q, R. Here l is atmospheric pressure, about 30 ft of water.
- The pressure is again l at the outlet EE.

At each junction Euler applies lossless Bernoulli: pressure plus velocity-height is continuous. Passing from area ff to gg the pressure therefore jumps by k^4 v(1/f^4 − 1/g^4).

§36 composes the per-tube exponential transfer with these Bernoulli jumps. This yields the chain P = l e^{−αa/f} + (f/α)(1−e^{−αa/f}) + k^4 v(1/f^4−1/g^4), Q = P e^{−αb/g} + (g/α)(1−e^{−αb/g}) cos ζ + k^4 v(1/g^4−1/h^4), and so on. The chain closes with l = R e^{−αd/i} + (i/α)(1−e^{−αd/i}) cos θ + k^4 v(1/i^4−1/k^4).

Each step is an affine map in the pressure, and every step is linear in v. Eliminating P, Q, R therefore gives one linear equation for v. The next page (§§37–38) does this elimination, writing e^{−αa/f} = 1−αA and so on. Euler remarks that the same law of composition serves for any number of segments.
errors: The first relation for P lacks the factor cos ε, although an angle ε was assigned to tube AF. The omission persists on the next page (P = (1−αA)l + Af + ...). It is correct only if AF is vertical, as in the earlier two-tube case: an inconsistency or oversight.
Physical gap: junctions are treated as lossless (pure Bernoulli). No loss at sudden expansion is included; that loss was later formulated by Borda (1766) and Carnot.

Physical gap: the underlying hypothesis that friction is proportional to absolute pressure is not borne out experimentally. It implies that atmospheric pressure l increases the frictional loss, which Euler stresses in §33. Later hydraulics (Chézy, Darcy–Weisbach) makes the loss depend on velocity, not ambient pressure.
The printed final line omits its left-hand side l ('= R e^{...}'); this is typographical.

ideas.what: Pressure decaying exponentially along a pipe because wall friction is taken proportional to local pressure; closed-form steady solution per inclined segment
ideas.modern_name: Linear first-order ODE for head along a pipe with a Coulomb-type wall-friction law
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E260) for this specific hypothesis; standard pipe-friction laws credited to Chézy, Darcy, Weisbach
ideas.where_published: E260 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 6), earlier sections

ideas.what: Series composition of pipe segments: affine pressure maps per segment plus Bernoulli jumps at area changes, closed by the outlet condition to give a linear equation for the efflux velocity-height
ideas.modern_name: Head-loss computation for pipes in series (transfer-map / recursive composition)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard hydraulics; general treatment of efflux through composite pipes goes back to Daniel Bernoulli's Hydrodynamica (1738) and Euler
ideas.where_published: E260; related composite-tube efflux problems in Euler's hydraulic papers (unsure of exact ones)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine generalisation of the preceding two-tube calculation to n segments under Euler's (physically mistaken) pressure-proportional friction law. The mathematics is elementary composition of affine maps. The only noteworthy detail is the missing cos ε factor, a small slip.
transcription_corrections: The angle for AF is ε; in the image it is partly obscured but consistent with ε.
The last equation begins with '=' in print; the intended left-hand side is l (outlet pressure equals atmospheric), i.e. l = R e^{−αd/i} + (i/α)(1−e^{−αd/i}) cos θ + k^4 v(1/i^4 − 1/k^4).
In the R line the print shows a stray 'c' before 'cof. η' ('...)c cof. η'); it should read '...) cos η'.
